about: Hand corrections for the Bench reaction show records (I-054, docs/loop/items/I-054/spec.md). The records are generated by crates/chem/src/show.rs from content/chem/core.json, substances.json and geometry.json by the rules in the spec; this file holds only what the rules cannot know: which reactions have a flame or a glow and what emits the light, where a reaction happens (in water, in air, in a melt), states that differ from the rules, how fast it goes, and visible changes the rules miss. Every entry says why. check is draft until the science review.

sources.SPEED: How fast each reaction goes on a bench: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e), chapters 4 and 12, and the Royal Society of Chemistry practical guides (https://edu.rsc.org/practical); speed classes are coarse (instant: under a second; fast: seconds to a minute; slow: minutes or longer, shown sped up).
sources.DEMO: The classroom demonstration as the Royal Society of Chemistry describes it (https://edu.rsc.org/experiments) and Shakhashiri, 'Chemical Demonstrations' vols. 1-4 (University of Wisconsin Press).
sources.MIST: A mist of water droplets looks white: droplets much larger than the wavelength of light scatter all visible wavelengths about equally (Bohren and Huffman, 'Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles', 1983). Steam itself is a colourless gas.
sources.AIR: Dry air is 78.08% N2 and 20.95% O2 by volume (with 0.93% Ar), taken here as O2 + 3.76 N2 (CRC Handbook, 'Composition of dry air').

Ca.note: Molecular bands of CaOH and CaO, not atomic lines.

Mg.note: Mostly white-hot MgO smoke particles, close to a blackbody, plus Mg emission.

Al.note: White-hot Al2O3 particles; aluminium powder burns like magnesium.

premixed.note: A gas burner flame with air mixed in: CH* (431 nm) and C2* Swan band (516 nm) emission, no soot.

soot.note: Glowing soot in a diffusion flame radiates close to a blackbody; the renderer can colour it from temp_k.

h2.note: OH* emits in the ultraviolet; in daylight the flame is nearly invisible.

alcohol.described: pale blue, hard to see in daylight

sulfur.note: Sulfur, hydrogen sulfide and carbon disulfide burn with a blue flame (S2* and SO2* emission).

nh3.note: NH2 alpha band emission; ammonia burns only in oxygen-rich air or pure oxygen.

methane_burns.why: natural gas burns in a burner with air mixed in

butane_burns.why: a gas burner flame (a camping stove)

hydrogen_burns.why: a hydrogen-air mix pops; the flame is almost invisible

candle_burns.why: a candle burns for hours with a yellow sooty flame

pentane_burns.why: a liquid fuel in a dish burns with a yellow diffusion flame

hexane_burns.why: a liquid fuel in a dish burns with a yellow diffusion flame

octane_burns.why: a liquid fuel in a dish burns with a yellow diffusion flame

ethene_burns.why: ethene burns with a luminous yellow flame

acetylene_burns.why: acetylene burns in air with a very sooty yellow flame

benzene_burns.why: benzene burns with a smoky yellow flame

methanol_burns.why: methanol burns with an almost invisible pale blue flame

ethanol_burns.why: ethanol burns with a pale blue flame

sulfur_burns.why: sulfur melts, then burns with a blue flame

co_burns.why: carbon monoxide burns with a blue flame

silane_burns.why: silane catches fire by itself in air; white silica smoke

phosphorus_burns.why: white phosphorus catches fire in air by itself

carbon_burns.why: charcoal glows orange-red rather than flaming

magnesium_burns.why: magnesium ribbon burns with a blinding white light

lithium_oxygen.why: lithium burns with a crimson flame

sodium_oxygen.why: sodium burns with a yellow-orange flame

calcium_oxygen.why: calcium burns with an orange-red flame

zinc_oxide.why: zinc burns in air with a bluish-green flame, giving white ZnO smoke

aluminium_oxide.why: aluminium powder burns with a brilliant white flame

silicon_oxygen.why: silicon glows white-hot as it burns

copper_oxide.why: copper does not burn; heated in air its surface turns black

salt_from_elements.why: hot sodium in chlorine burns with a bright yellow flame and white NaCl smoke

potassium_chlorine.why: potassium burns in chlorine with a lilac flame

magnesium_chlorine.why: magnesium burns in chlorine with a white flame

aluminium_chlorine.why: aluminium glows in chlorine, giving white AlCl3 smoke

copper_chlorine.why: hot copper glows in chlorine, giving brown-yellow CuCl2 smoke

iron_chlorine.why: hot iron wool glows in chlorine, giving brown FeCl3 smoke

sodium_bromine.why: sodium reacts slowly with bromine, even warm

iron_sulfur.why: once started, a red glow spreads through the iron and sulfur mixture

copper_sulfur.why: a glow spreads through the mixture

zinc_sulfur.why: zinc and sulfur react violently in a flash with smoke

magnesium_co2.why: magnesium keeps burning in carbon dioxide, leaving black specks of carbon

magnesium_steam.why: magnesium burns in steam with a white flame

lithium_nitrogen.why: lithium slowly turns red-brown in nitrogen at room temperature

sodium_hydride.note: Little to see: hot sodium takes up hydrogen gas and becomes a grey-white powder.

hydrogen_sulfur.note: Little to see: molten sulfur takes up hydrogen; the gas made is colourless and smells of rotten eggs.

potassium_water.why: potassium on water lights the hydrogen with a lilac flame

sodium_water.note: The sodium melts into a fizzing silvery ball that skates on the water.

calcium_water.note: Calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble, so the water turns cloudy white.

thermite.why: thermite burns white-hot with sparks and leaves molten iron

copper_oxide_carbon.why: the mixture glows as the black powder turns pink-brown

copper_oxide_hydrogen.why: the black powder glows and turns pink; water drips on the cool glass

zinc_oxide_carbon.why: at the furnace temperature zinc comes off as a vapour

nitrogen_triiodide.note: Touching the dry solid sets off a sharp crack and a puff of violet iodine vapour.

hcl_synthesis.note: In bright light the mixture explodes; the yellow-green colour vanishes.

hf_synthesis.note: Explodes even in the dark and cold.

hbr_synthesis.why: bromine vapour and hydrogen react hot

methane_chlorine.why: the yellow-green colour fades in light

salt_electrolysis.why: the salt is melted (molten) for this

alumina_electrolysis.note: The alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite at about 1230 K.

limestone_roast.why: lime glows brilliantly white when strongly heated (limelight)

glass_making.note: Carbon dioxide bubbles up through the glowing melt.

ostwald_1.note: The platinum catalyst gauze stays red-hot by itself once started.

potassium_chlorate_heat.note: The chlorate melts first, then oxygen bubbles out of the melt.

mercury_oxide_heat.note: Silvery droplets of mercury collect on the cool glass.

ammonium_chloride_heat.note: The white solid seems to vanish, then white smoke reforms on the cool glass as the gases join again.

neutralise_ammonia_hcl.note: Where the two gases meet, a white smoke of ammonium chloride forms.
neutralise_ammonia_hcl.why: the classic gas-diffusion demonstration (a white ring in a tube)

so3_water.note: Sulfur trioxide meets water violently, making a fog of sulfuric acid droplets.
so3_water.why: why industry dissolves SO3 in acid instead

p4o10_water.note: The white powder hisses as it dissolves; the water gets hot.
p4o10_water.why: phosphorus oxide is a drying agent

slaking_lime.note: The lumps hiss, swell and crumble; the heat boils some of the water into steam.

co2_water.note: Nothing to see: the gas dissolves. An indicator would show the water turning slightly acidic.

so2_water.note: Nothing to see: the gas dissolves into an acidic solution.

ammonia_water.note: Nothing to see: the gas dissolves very readily and the water warms.

sodium_oxide_water.note: The white solid dissolves and the water warms.

speed: a few seconds after a drop of water
aluminium_iodine.note: A drop of water starts it; after a pause, violet iodine vapour puffs up and the mix may flame.

zinc_iodine.why: the brown iodine colour fades as the mixture warms

photosynthesis.note: In pondweed, small bubbles of oxygen rise from the leaves in light.

speed: all the time, in every cell
respiration.note: Happens inside living cells: nothing to see in a flask.

sucrose_hydrolysis.note: Nothing to see: the sugar solution stays clear.
sucrose_hydrolysis.why: an enzyme or acid does it

peroxide_splits.note: With a catalyst, the liquid froths with oxygen.

ozone_forms.note: Nothing to see: ozone is colourless at this strength, but it has a sharp smell.

lightning_nitrogen.note: Nothing to see at first: nitric oxide is colourless (it turns brown later in air).

no_oxidises.why: colourless nitric oxide turns brown at once in air

nitrogen_dioxide_dimer.note: The brown gas fades as it cools; warming brings the colour back.

haber.note: Nothing to see: colourless gases in a steel reactor.

contact_so3.note: Nothing to see inside the converter; SO3 fumes white in moist air.

ostwald_3.why: the brown gas dissolves in water

steam_reforming.why: an industrial plant; the water is steam

methanol_synthesis.note: Nothing to see: colourless gases and liquid.

urea_synthesis.note: White urea comes out of a colourless melt.

ethene_water.note: Nothing to see: colourless gases and vapour.

ethene_bromine.why: bromine water turns colourless when ethene is bubbled through: the classic test for a double bond

esterification.note: A fruity smell; the liquids stay colourless.
esterification.why: an ester smells of pear drops; it is heated under reflux, so the products stay liquid

ethanol_dehydration.note: Colourless gas comes off; nothing else to see.

cracking.note: Colourless vapour over the hot catalyst.

magnesium_carbonate_heat.note: Little to see: one white powder becomes another as the gas leaves.

marble_sulfuric.note: The fizzing soon stops: insoluble calcium sulfate coats the marble.
marble_sulfuric.why: the classic example of a reaction that stops

mgo_acid.note: The white powder dissolves and the solution warms slightly.

co2_naoh.note: Nothing to see: the gas is absorbed.

bleach_making.why: chlorine gas bubbles into the alkali and its colour fades

copper_nitric.note: The gas made is colourless nitric oxide, which turns brown as soon as it meets air.

neutralise_hcl_naoh.note: Two colourless solutions mix and stay colourless; the mixture warms a little.

neutralise_hcl_koh.note: Colourless solutions; the mixture warms a little.

neutralise_hcl_lioh.note: Colourless solutions; the mixture warms a little.

neutralise_hno3_naoh.note: Colourless solutions; the mixture warms a little.

neutralise_hno3_koh.note: Colourless solutions; the mixture warms a little.

neutralise_caoh2_hcl.note: Colourless solutions; the mixture warms a little.

neutralise_vinegar_naoh.note: Colourless solutions; the mixture warms a little.

lab_ammonia.note: A sharp-smelling colourless gas comes off; water condenses near the mouth of the tube.

baking_soda_heat.note: Water droplets condense at the cool end of the tube.

lime_dries.note: Water vapour comes off and condenses on cool glass.
